html:
The Issyk kurgan is a burial mound near the town of Issyk, about 50 km east of Almaty in Kazakhstan. Soviet archaeologists led by Kemal Akishev opened it in 1969 and found a young warrior dressed in gold, now called the Golden Man. The burial dates to about the 4th or 3rd century BCE.

The dead person belonged to the Saka, the horse riding nomads of the steppe. The main chamber had been missed by robbers. The body wore a jacket, belt and boots sewn with thousands of small gold plaques, and a tall pointed headdress decorated with arrows, snow leopards and winged horses, in the steppe animal style. Some scholars now argue the person may have been a woman.

A silver cup in the grave carries a short inscription in a script no one has fully read, one of the oldest pieces of writing found in Central Asia.

After independence in 1991, Kazakhstan made the Golden Man a national symbol. A statue of him stands on the Independence Monument in Almaty. Like the frozen tombs of Pazyryk, it shows the wealth and skill of the steppe peoples.
